planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into consistently wet, peaty, acidic soil in full shade, mimicking its native evergreen-swamp and bog-margin habitat.

directions: Fine, weeping, thread-like foliage sets this sedge apart in deep shade and acidic, humus-rich wet soil where few other sedges perform. It tolerates standing water seasonally but resents summer drought, so it is best under tree cover with a reliable moisture source rather than in open sun. Use it as a texture plant threaded through ferns and Sphagnum-adjacent plantings rather than as a standalone specimen.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into acidic, non-calcareous, consistently moist soil in a bog garden, container water feature, or pond margin with light afternoon shade.

directions: Pale, waxy, silvery-green foliage gives this sedge a distinct color note among the green sedges already in cultivation. It is intolerant of lime, unlike many wetland sedges, so give it acidic, non-calcareous soil with consistent moisture. Site it where it gets good light in spring but some relief from peak summer heat, since performance declines once summer temperatures climb; its semi-evergreen, silvery wand-like seed heads give late-spring interest.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge, thicket, or streambank in part shade; allow arching stems room to touch down and root.

directions: This sedge naturally self-layers, with arching stems rooting wherever they touch ground, making it a good spreading groundcover for damp shaded sites without being aggressively rhizomatous. Give it room to form expanding colonies along a woodland edge, thicket, or streambank in part shade, since this vegetative spread is how the species naturally behaves rather than staying in a tidy clump. Combine with ferns and other wetland sedges along creek banks or shaded swales.

common_name: Yellow Fox Sedge (Small Yellow Fox Sedge)

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant in full sun in soil ranging from consistently wet to average garden moisture, at the drier margins of a rain garden.

directions: Golden-yellow seed heads give this sedge a warm color accent most sedges lack, peaking in late spring to midsummer and providing food for birds and waterfowl. It is more drought-adaptable than most wetland Carex, making it useful at the drier margins of a rain garden where plantings transition to mesic companions. Good along ditches, pond edges, and seasonally flooded spots where a sun-loving, easy-care sedge is wanted.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant in full sun with saturated or standing-water soil along a lake, river shore, marsh margin, or constructed pond edge.

directions: An obligate-wetland sedge dominant across much of North America, this species produces bold, toppling seed spikes that give it a loose, informal look rather than a tidy clump during its June-July bloom, so plant it where that cascading habit reads as a feature on a naturalized shoreline. It is one of the most widely distributed North American sedges, reading as regionally appropriate well beyond New England. It was historically treated under the older name Carex rostrata by some floras and nurseries.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into consistently moist to wet, open ground such as a sunny rain garden or low-mow wet meadow.

directions: Native to Appalachian and Northeastern wet meadows, ditches, and stream edges, this sedge fills a niche between showier wood sedges and larger wetland sedges for a region-specific rain garden palette. It tolerates some human-disturbed or maintained conditions better than more specialist bog sedges, making it a reasonable choice for wetter residential sites. Pair it with other Northeastern wet-meadow natives rather than true bog specialists, since it doesn't require the acidic peat that more exacting bog sedges need.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into a constructed bog garden or acidic pond-edge substrate with Sphagnum-type conditions; will not perform in ordinary garden loam.

directions: A true peat-bog specialist with documented Indigenous ethnobotanical use, this sedge needs consistently saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor soil and will not perform in ordinary garden loam even if kept wet. Best reserved for a constructed bog garden, an acidic pond-edge planting, or a restoration project rather than a general rain garden. It takes full sun in cool, boreal-leaning climates, with some afternoon relief helpful at the southern edge of its range.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into full sun to light shade with reliably wet to saturated soil, such as a pond edge or rain garden.

directions: Only named cultivars of this species were previously represented in this dataset — the plain wild species itself is one of the most sun-tolerant fine-leaved sedges and one of the most wet-tolerant sedges in cultivation generally, native to blackwater streams from Michigan and Nova Scotia south to Florida and Texas. Its extremely narrow, weeping foliage makes a strong textural contrast plant for pond edges and rain gardens, and it is semi-evergreen to evergreen in milder zones. Cultivation notes parallel the cultivars already in the dataset closely, since this is essentially their parent species.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
